extracted.intended_audience: research funders, grant peer reviewers, interdisciplinary researchers, research managers and policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for assessing interdisciplinary research proposals (and implications for publication/hiring assessment), focusing on what makes peer review appropriate for interdisciplinary work and how reviewers/organisations should be organised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of the topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing significance involves evaluating the importance of the issue being addressed against some measure such as government research priorities, the prevalence of the problem or its likely impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments may set priority areas; applicants strengthen the case by, for example, highlighting the number of people affected or potential cost savings. The same assessment criteria are relevant for both discipline-based and interdisciplinary research: research with a clear case for significance is more likely to be funded than arcane research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance and tractability of the research question
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the unknowns being tackled, especially whether they are critical unknowns likely to yield productive outcomes, taking into account what is already known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplines have norms about which unknowns are the business of that discipline; becoming a disciplinary expert includes learning which unknowns to tackle. Interdisciplinary proposals should be assessed on the nature and tractability of the unknowns they target rather than only by disciplinary norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of the types of 'unknowns' in interdisciplinary research
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary research can embody different approaches to unknowns that reviewers should recognise and evaluate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Six illustrative types: (1) combining separate disciplinary unknowns addressed within respective disciplines; (2) addressing unknowns outside the business of any discipline but important to stakeholders; (3) tackling unknowns marginalised by power imbalances; (4) investigating unknowns in overlaps between disciplines; (5) identifying unknowns critical to the problem but little studied by disciplines; (6) recognising and managing intractable unknowns that cannot be solved but pose risks/unintended consequences. Reviewers should judge whether the proposal identifies which kinds of unknowns it addresses and uses appropriate approaches for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of the methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Two essential strands: are the methods appropriate for the unknowns being tackled, and are they currently the best available methods?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For interdisciplinary work this includes evaluating how disciplinary insights are integrated, how intractable unknowns are dealt with, and how disciplines and stakeholders are chosen. Unlike disciplines, there is no established, widely-accepted set of interdisciplinary methods, which complicates assessment. Reviewers should therefore consider both fit-to-problem and whether methods reflect current best practice (recognising that identifying 'best' methods may be hampered by fragmented knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: synthesis of disciplinary and stakeholder knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how the proposal plans to synthesise disciplinary evidence and stakeholder knowledge as part of its methodological approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author identifies this as one of three main domains for a repository of interdisciplinary methods; reviewers should look for explicit plans and questions addressing knowledge synthesis (and whether appropriate synthesis methods are proposed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: understanding and managing diverse unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the project has methods to understand, categorise and manage the diverse kinds of unknowns that arise in interdisciplinary problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This domain includes scoping which unknowns are tractable versus which require risk-management, and methods to surface marginalized or stakeholder-generated unknowns. Proposals should show how they will handle intractable or high-uncertainty issues rather than ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: providing integrated research support for policy and practice change
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether methods provide integrated research support aimed at informing policy and practice change where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdisciplinary research tackling complex problems often has applied aims; reviewers should check whether methods integrate knowledge and unknowns to produce outputs usable for policy/practice and whether this integration is credible and planned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoping, boundary setting and context examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the proposal's approach to scoping the problem, setting boundaries (which disciplines/stakeholders to include) and examining the context of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's proposed repository includes five key questions per domain, including scoping and boundary setting and context examination. Reviewers should look for clear rationale for inclusion/exclusion of disciplines/stakeholders and an articulated problem context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of applicants (general: track record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Past success, especially in the recent past, is used as a guide to the likelihood of future success; competence is assessed on applicants' track records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers commonly look for several concrete indicators (see separate entries). Interdisciplinary norms for track record may differ from disciplinary norms and should be contextualised by reviewers experienced in interdisciplinarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence: publication record and venue quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers look for the number of peer-reviewed papers and the quality of journals in which they are published (or number of books and quality of the publisher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is concern that interdisciplinary research has fewer appropriate high-quality outlets; reviewers should take into account disciplinary differences in publication norms and the limited availability of venue 'fit' for interdisciplinary methods and outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence: past success in attracting competitive funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers consider applicants' record of securing competitive grants as evidence of capability to deliver research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past funding success is a common proxy for likely future success, but reviewers should interpret this in context (e.g., interdisciplinary researchers may have different funding histories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence: evidence of effective team collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that at least some team members have worked together successfully in the past is valued, especially for team-based disciplinary or interdisciplinary research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdisciplinary teams face a wider range of both 'good' differences (to harness) and 'bad' differences (to manage) than disciplinary teams; reviewers should look for evidence of prior successful collaboration and plans for team management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence: research impact on policy and practice (including commercialization)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is growing interest in adding demonstrable research impact on policy and practice change (including commercialization) to assessments of competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where relevant, reviewers should evaluate whether the team has achieved prior impact or has credible pathways to impact. This may advantage interdisciplinary teams but must be judged with appropriate evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teamwork and collaboration management
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the proposal recognises and plans to harness productive disciplinary differences and manage problematic differences (including personality differences) that can stymie partnership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective collaboration involves management plans for communication, roles, conflict resolution and integration. Given the greater diversity in interdisciplinary teams, reviewers should look for explicit management strategies and evidence they are likely to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection: need for reviewers experienced in similar interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary research needs to be assessed by peers who have themselves undertaken similar kinds of interdisciplinary research and therefore understand the importance of different kinds of unknowns and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding such reviewers is challenging because interdisciplinarity is unorganized; where possible panels should include reviewers with direct interdisciplinary experience in the problem area and without conflicts of interest. Review processes should recognise reviewer expertise beyond single disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation of interdisciplinarity: colleges of peers and professional associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate peer review will only occur if interdisciplinarity is 'organised' through colleges of peers and professional associations that agree assessment criteria and norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The current fragmented small associations limit the ability to find competent peers and to establish agreed norms; funders and the interdisciplinary community should consider actions to build organizational structures and shared criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit criterion: 'zing' (innovative edge)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tacit element called 'zing' is an innovative edge that can lift a proposal above a pack of solid research and make the difference in funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not discussed in depth, reviewers and applicants should recognise that novelty/transformative potential can be decisive when many proposals are otherwise sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess tractability versus risk: recognise and plan for intractable unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary proposals should identify which unknowns are intractable and describe how potential risks and unintended consequences will be identified, monitored and mitigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some risks can be addressed by targeted research; others cannot be definitively solved but require mitigation strategies and monitoring. Reviewers should expect proposals to address both solvable and intractable risks explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for agreed criteria across assessment contexts (grants, publications, hiring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinarity requires establishing appropriate criteria not only for grant peer review but also for publication review and performance assessment for hiring and career advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria must be recognised and agreed by the interdisciplinary community before they can serve as the basis for effective review processes; reviewers and institutions should work to develop and adopt such norms.
